# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Re:** Fatesk Interactive Entertainment, LLC / Drupuv Systems, Inc. – Nimbus Platform License: pre-signature issues list
**Date:** November 10, 2026
**Privileged & Confidential – Attorney Work Product**

---

## 1. Bottom Line

The execution drafts depart from the agreed term sheet in four ways that matter. In each case the departure works against Fatesk.

1. **Severity 1 protections are largely hollowed out.** The SLA Schedule's much narrower "Severity 1 Incident" definition overrides the License Agreement's definition through the precedence clause. Fatesk's one-hour response commitment and its chronic-failure termination right would then apply only to a total, global outage.
2. **Drupuv can assign the deal to anyone, including a Fatesk competitor, without consent.** That buyer would also take over Fatesk's player account, commerce and telemetry data.
3. **The deal auto-renews for three-year terms.** Fatesk can only opt out in a 30-day window, and renewal fees can rise up to 9%. One missed window commits Fatesk to roughly **$5.5–$6.0 million** of further fees.
4. **Implementation disputes are split off into California law and San Francisco courts.** The License Agreement says Delaware law and Wilmington courts. Because the SOW controls as to Implementation Services, a single failed-launch dispute could be split across two laws and two exclusive forums.

The economics are significant. The annual license fee is **$1,840,000 per contract year** (License Agreement §5.1), and the implementation fee is a **$420,000 fixed fee** (SOW §5.1). Over the three-year Initial Term, the committed spend is about **$5.94 million** before any overage.

**One structural point runs through Issues 1 and 4.** License Agreement §17.4 (Order of Precedence) provides that, if the documents conflict, they prevail in this order:

- first, **the SOW (as to Implementation Services)**;
- then **the SLA Schedule (as to service levels and incident classification)**;
- then the License Agreement.

In other words, the License Agreement sits at the *bottom* of the hierarchy within those subject areas. That is the mechanism that lets the SOW's governing-law clause and the SLA Schedule's severity definition override the main agreement. Fixing §17.4 is the single most efficient markup.

**Documents reviewed:**

| Document | Relevance |
|---|---|
| Platform License Agreement (execution draft) | Core |
| Implementation Statement of Work | Core |
| Service Level Schedule | Core |
| Term sheet (Nov. 6, 2026; non-binding except §§14–15) | Benchmark for what was agreed commercially |
| Wilmington studio office lease (Christina Landing Office Partners, LLC) | **No bearing on this deal.** It shares Fatesk's notice address and Delaware governing law, but creates no rights or obligations relevant to the Drupuv license. Not analyzed further. |

---

## 2. Issues, in Order of Priority

### Issue 1 – "Severity 1 Incident": the SLA Schedule's narrow definition overrides the License Agreement

**Where it appears**

- **Service Level Schedule §2.1(a)** defines "Severity 1 Incident" as "complete unavailability of the Platform to all End Users **in all regions**."
- **The closing sentence of SLA §2.1** states that the severity classifications "apply **for all purposes of the Agreement**."
- **License Agreement §1.11** defines Severity 1 Incident as an incident making matchmaking, login or in-game purchases unavailable to **10% or more of End Users**. This matches term sheet §5.2.
- **License Agreement §17.4** makes the SLA Schedule prevail over the License Agreement "as to service levels and incident classification."
- The Severity 1 definition drives these provisions:
  - License Agreement §7.2: one-hour response, continuous senior engineering, hourly updates.
  - License Agreement §7.4: root cause analysis within 5 business days.
  - License Agreement §8.4: termination for 3+ Severity 1 Incidents in any rolling 90 days, with refund of prepaid fees.
  - License Agreement §17.5: force majeure does not excuse §7.2.
  - SLA §3.3 (immediate escalation) and SLA §4.1 (4-hour workaround and 12-hour resolution targets).

**Why it matters for Fatesk**

Read together, these provisions put the SLA's "all End Users in all regions" test in control. That conflict sits squarely within "incident classification," and Drupuv will say the SLA's "for all purposes" language confirms it.

None of the following would be a Severity 1 Incident under that test:

- a full North America outage;
- a login-only failure across every platform;
- a storefront outage that stops all in-game purchases on launch day;
- a failure confined to one first-party platform (e.g., PlayStation).

SLA §2.1(b) expressly pushes regional and platform-specific outages into **Severity 2**. Severity 2 carries:

- a 2-hour response;
- no mandatory root cause analysis unless Fatesk requests one;
- **no termination right**.

Practically, these are the outages that hurt a live-service publisher, especially during the launch windows Fatesk negotiated for. On the drafts as written:

- the §8.4 chronic-failure exit becomes almost impossible to trigger, because three complete global outages in 90 days is unrealistic;
- the commercial protections in term sheet §§5.2–5.4 are effectively lost.

**Recommended fix**

1. Replace SLA §2.1(a) with the License Agreement definition:
   > "(a) '**Severity 1 Incident**' has the meaning given in Section 1.11 of the Agreement, namely an incident making matchmaking, login or in-game purchases unavailable to ten percent (10%) or more of End Users, whether in one or more Regions or on one or more first-party platforms."
2. Conform SLA §2.1(b) so that Severity 2 covers only incidents that are **not** Severity 1 under the Agreement definition. Delete the reference to regional and first-party outages, or limit it to outages affecting fewer than 10% of End Users.
3. Delete "The severity classifications in this Section 2.1 apply for all purposes of the Agreement," or replace it with: "In the event of any inconsistency, the definition of 'Severity 1 Incident' in Section 1.11 of the Agreement controls."
4. Belt-and-braces: amend License Agreement §17.4 so that the definitions in License Agreement §1 and Sections 7.2, 7.4 and 8.4 prevail over the SLA Schedule (see the consolidated §17.4 language in Issue 4).

**Negotiating position:** non-negotiable. This is the agreed term sheet definition. Drupuv cannot credibly argue that a new, narrower definition was a commercial point.

---

### Issue 2 – Unrestricted assignment by Drupuv ("Permitted Transfer" reaches any person, including a competitor)

**Where it appears**

- **License Agreement §15.2**: Drupuv may assign "in whole or in part, without Fatesk's consent **in connection with a Permitted Transfer**." The only obligation is notice within 30 days *after* the assignment takes effect.
- **License Agreement §1.8**: "Permitted Transfer" means "any merger, change of control, or sale of all or any part of the business or assets to which this Agreement relates, **to any person**."
- **Contrast with License Agreement §15.1**: Fatesk cannot assign without Drupuv's consent.
- **Term sheet §10.2**: "Drupuv may not assign to a Fatesk competitor without Fatesk's prior written consent."

**Why it matters for Fatesk**

- **Competitor access to sensitive data.** As drafted, Drupuv can transfer this Agreement to a rival publisher, or to a platform owned by one, without asking. That transferee would host and operate Fatesk's:
  - End User accounts, entitlements and virtual currency balances;
  - purchase records;
  - matchmaking data and telemetry (Fatesk Data, License Agreement §1.4);
  - information on unreleased titles and player metrics (License Agreement §11.3).

  Contractual data-use limits in License Agreement §9.1 help, but they are no substitute for keeping a competitor out of the operator seat.
- **Partial transfers.** "All **or any part**" of the business, plus assignment "in whole or in part," lets Drupuv carve up the deal. For example, it could sell the commerce service to one buyer and keep matchmaking. Fatesk would then face fragmented counterparties and SLA accountability.
- **No veto and no exit.** Notice comes only after closing. Fatesk has no termination right on a Drupuv change of control.
- **Drift from the term sheet.** This is a clear departure from term sheet §10.2.

**Recommended fix**

1. Narrow the definition in License Agreement §1.8:
   > "'**Permitted Transfer**' means a merger, change of control, or sale of all or substantially all of Drupuv's business or assets to which this Agreement relates, to a person that (a) is not a Fatesk Competitor and is not controlled by a Fatesk Competitor, and (b) assumes in writing all of Drupuv's obligations under this Agreement."
2. Add a definition of "**Fatesk Competitor**": any person, or Affiliate of a person, that publishes or develops video games for commercial distribution, together with any entity listed in a schedule Fatesk may update annually.
3. Revise License Agreement §15.2:
   - assignment of the Agreement "in whole only";
   - **Fatesk's prior written consent required for any assignment or change of control involving a Fatesk Competitor**;
   - at least 30 days' **advance** notice of any Permitted Transfer.
4. Add a **termination right on a Drupuv change of control**. Fatesk may terminate on notice within 120 days after notice of the change of control. On termination:
   - Fatesk receives a refund of prepaid fees;
   - the License Agreement §12.5 transition period applies at no increase in fees;
   - the License Agreement §9.5 data export and deletion obligations apply.

**Negotiating position:** the competitor consent right is term sheet language and should be held. The change-of-control termination right is an ask. It is reasonable given the data at stake, and we could trade it for a longer notice period if Drupuv pushes back.

---

### Issue 3 – Automatic three-year renewal with a narrow 30-day opt-out window

**Where it appears**

- **License Agreement §12.2**: after the three-year Initial Term (License Agreement §12.1), the Agreement "shall renew automatically for **successive three (3) year Renewal Terms**." A non-renewal notice is effective only if delivered "**no earlier than one hundred fifty (150) days** and no later than one hundred twenty (120) days before the end of the then-current term."
- **License Agreement §5.3**: Drupuv may raise the annual license fee by up to **9%** at each renewal, on 180 days' notice.
- **Term sheet §8.2**: "one-year renewals; either party may decline renewal on 90 days' notice before term end." The term sheet does not provide for any renewal fee increase.

**Why it matters for Fatesk**

- **The opt-out window is a trap.** Fatesk has a single 30-day window. Assuming the Initial Term ends January 31, 2030, the window runs roughly **September 3 to October 3, 2029**. Notice sent too early is as ineffective as notice sent too late.
- **A missed window is expensive.** It locks Fatesk into three more years of fees:
  - **$5,520,000** at the current $1,840,000 rate; or
  - about **$6,016,800** if Drupuv takes the full 9% increase.
- **Compounding exposure.** The cycle repeats every three years, and each renewal can carry a new increase of up to 9%.
- **Loss of flexibility.** For a publisher whose title slate and platform needs may change, the term sheet's one-year renewals with 90 days' notice were an important commercial protection. The draft removes it.

**Recommended fix**

1. Replace License Agreement §12.2:
   > "12.2 **Renewal.** After the Initial Term, this Agreement shall renew automatically for successive one (1) year Renewal Terms unless either Party gives the other written notice of non-renewal at least ninety (90) days before the end of the then-current term."

   This deletes the "no earlier than" floor, so notice can be given at any time up to 90 days before term end.
2. Revise License Agreement §5.3:
   - cap any renewal increase at the lesser of **3%** or CPI, or delete the increase right entirely since the term sheet did not provide for one;
   - keep the 180-day advance notice, so that Fatesk knows the price before its non-renewal deadline.
3. Fallback if Drupuv insists on auto-renewal mechanics: require Drupuv to send a written renewal reminder 60 days before the non-renewal deadline. Non-renewal would not be deemed waived until 30 days after that reminder.

**Internal action:** whatever the outcome, we should docket the non-renewal deadline with Fatesk's legal operations team at signing.

---

### Issue 4 – Governing law and forum: the SOW's California law and San Francisco courts override Delaware for implementation disputes

**Where it appears**

- **SOW §9.1**: the SOW and "any dispute arising out of or relating to this SOW **or the Implementation Services**" are governed by "the **laws of the State of California**."
- **SOW §9.2**: "exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in **San Francisco County**, California."
- **License Agreement §17.1 and §17.2**: Delaware law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in Wilmington, Delaware. This matches term sheet §12.
- **License Agreement §17.4**: the SOW prevails "as to Implementation Services."

**Why it matters for Fatesk**

- **Delaware does not govern implementation disputes.** Because License Agreement §17.4 gives the SOW precedence for Implementation Services, the SOW's choice of California law and an exclusive San Francisco forum would control implementation disputes. The Implementation Services are tightly bound up with the licensed Platform (SOW §2):
  - SDK integration;
  - matchmaking and commerce configuration;
  - data migration of Ironveil account, entitlement and currency data;
  - load testing at the Licensed Concurrency;
  - launch war-room support.
- **Related claims get split.** A typical failed-launch scenario would generate claims under both documents. For example, integration code fails under load, the Platform goes down, migrated balances are corrupted, and Fatesk wants service credits, damages and termination. The result:
  - SLA and License Agreement claims (credits, §8.4 termination, §14 liability) go to Wilmington under Delaware law;
  - SOW and Implementation Services claims (milestone acceptance, §13.2(b) workmanship warranty as applied through SOW §10.3, migration failures) go to San Francisco under California law;
  - each clause is "exclusive," so neither court can necessarily hear the whole dispute.
- **Consequences for Fatesk:**
  - parallel litigation and duplicated cost;
  - risk of inconsistent rulings;
  - threshold fights over which forum and which law apply to each claim;
  - a possible argument that California law governs how the shared License Agreement terms apply to implementation claims, including the liability cap, the exclusions and the warranty disclaimer.
- **Drift from the term sheet.** Term sheet §12 provided that the Definitive Agreements, which include the SOW, would be governed by Delaware law with Wilmington courts. Both parties are Delaware entities and Fatesk is based in Wilmington. California has no evident connection to Fatesk.

**Recommended fix**

1. Conform SOW §9 to Delaware:
   > "9.1 **Governing Law and Forum.** This SOW is governed by Sections 17.1 and 17.2 of the Agreement. Any dispute arising out of or relating to this SOW or the Implementation Services shall be governed by the laws of the State of Delaware and resolved exclusively in the state and federal courts located in Wilmington, Delaware."
2. Amend License Agreement §17.4 so that the SOW's and SLA Schedule's precedence is limited to operational and commercial specifics:
   > "17.4 **Order of Precedence.** If there is a conflict among the documents forming this Agreement, the SOW shall prevail solely as to the scope, schedule, milestones, acceptance criteria and fees for the Implementation Services, and the SLA Schedule shall prevail solely as to service level metrics, measurement and service credits; otherwise this License Agreement prevails. Notwithstanding the foregoing, Sections 1 (Definitions), 7.2, 7.4, 8.4, 9, 12, 14, 15 and 17 of this License Agreement prevail over any conflicting provision of the SOW or the SLA Schedule, and no SOW or schedule may vary them unless it expressly identifies the Section being varied and is signed by both Parties."

   This single change also backstops Issues 1 and 2.

**Negotiating position:** a clean-up point grounded in the term sheet. We expect little resistance unless Drupuv's implementation team operates out of California and its counsel wants home courts. If so, hold Delaware for everything. Splitting forums is worse for Fatesk than either single forum.

---

## 3. Secondary Points for the Markup

These are lower priority, but worth raising in the same turn.

| # | Location | Point | Suggested position |
|---|---|---|---|
| a | SOW §4.2 | Deemed acceptance: a milestone is deemed accepted if Fatesk misses the 10-business-day review and does not respond within 5 business days of a reminder. | Require reminders to go to the Fatesk project manager and the General Counsel. Deemed acceptance should not override §4.1's "no open Severity 1/2 defects" and "no unresolved discrepancies" conditions. |
| b | SOW §3.1 | Milestones are only "commercially reasonable efforts," with no remedy for delay. | Add firm dates for M3 and M4 tied to the Project Halcyon launch, with fee holdbacks or delay credits. |
| c | SLA §7.5(c) | First-party platform outages are excluded "where the Platform is otherwise operating normally." | Acceptable in principle. Confirm the exclusion does not reach failures in Drupuv's integration with first-party identity and storefront services. |
| d | SLA §7.4 | Service credits are capped at 50% of the Monthly Fee. | Consider asking for 100% in launch-window months to match the doubling in SLA §7.3. |
| e | License Agreement §14.5 | Liability cap equals 12 months' fees, consistent with the term sheet. | No change, provided the §14.6 carve-outs (data, confidentiality) survive. |

---

## 4. Open Questions for the Client Call

1. **Term sheet concessions.** Did Fatesk's business team agree to any of these changes after November 6, 2026? In particular: three-year renewals, the 9% uplift, the SLA severity definition, or California law. If so, we need to know before positioning these items as "term sheet" points.
2. **Competitor list.** Which companies does Fatesk regard as competitors? Is Fatesk aware of any pending sale or financing of Drupuv, or of any acquirer interest? This determines how hard we push the change-of-control exit.
3. **Outage profile.** What outage scope does Fatesk consider launch-critical: a single Region, a single first-party platform, or a single Core Service? This calibrates whether the 10% threshold is right, or whether Fatesk wants regional or platform triggers expressly included.
4. **Launch timing.** What are the target launch dates for Project Halcyon and the Ironveil migration? This bears on the milestone dates (point 3(b)) and on how much the SOW forum issue matters in practice.
5. **California connection.** Does Fatesk have any California presence, or any reason to accept California law (for example, a California-based co-development studio under License Agreement §2.3)? We are assuming it does not.
6. **Term end date.** "Three years from the Effective Date" could be read as ending January 31, 2030 or February 1, 2030. We should confirm with Drupuv and state an express end date so the non-renewal deadline is certain.
7. **Termination for convenience.** Does Fatesk want a termination-for-convenience right during any Renewal Term? This would be an alternative fallback if Drupuv resists one-year renewals.

---

**Proposed next step:** with your sign-off, I will prepare a redline of License Agreement §§1.8, 5.3, 12.2, 15.2 and 17.4, SOW §9 and SLA §2.1 reflecting the fixes above. I will also prepare a short cover email to Drupuv's counsel framing Issues 1–4 as conforming changes to the term sheet.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Re:** Fatesk Interactive Entertainment, LLC / Drupuv Systems, Inc.: Nimbus Platform License, pre-signature issues list
**Date:** November 10, 2026

---

## 1. Bottom Line

The execution drafts mostly follow the November 6, 2026 term sheet on commercial terms. These include the $1,840,000 annual license fee, the 750,000 Licensed Concurrency, the $420,000 fixed implementation fee, data ownership and the liability structure. Three drafting choices, however, depart from the term sheet in ways that hurt Fatesk materially. We should fix all three before signature:

1. **Split governing law and forum.** The SOW selects California law and San Francisco courts. The License Agreement's precedence clause lets the SOW win on Implementation Services.
2. **Severity 1 definition hollowed out.** The SLA Schedule's narrow "Severity 1 Incident" definition controls over the License Agreement's definition. This strips Fatesk's one-hour response protection and its chronic-failure termination right.
3. **Three-year evergreen renewal with a 30-day opt-out window.** The term sheet agreed one-year renewals with 90 days' notice.

Section 4 lists secondary points for the markup. Section 5 lists open questions for the client call.

**Documents reviewed:**
- the License Agreement (D1);
- the Implementation SOW (D2);
- the term sheet (D3);
- the SLA Schedule (D4); and
- the Wilmington studio office lease (D5).

The lease is a separate real estate arrangement with an unrelated landlord. It does not bear on the license deal, and I have not analyzed it further. Its Delaware governing law and Wilmington address are coincidental.

---

## 2. Key Structural Point: The Order of Precedence (D1 § 17.4)

Two of the three priority issues depend on D1 Section 17.4. If the documents conflict, they "prevail in the following order":

1. the SOW (as to Implementation Services);
2. then the SLA Schedule (as to service levels and incident classification);
3. then the License Agreement.

The License Agreement therefore sits at the bottom. Any conflicting term in the SOW or SLA Schedule overrides it within their subject areas. Drupuv's counsel appears to have used this structure to move key terms out of the License Agreement. The fix is to narrow Section 17.4 so the License Agreement prevails on core legal and risk-allocation terms.

---

## 3. Priority Issues

### Issue 1: Severity 1 Incident definition gutted by the SLA Schedule (highest commercial risk)

**Where it appears:**
- D4 (SLA Schedule) Section 2.1(a), plus the closing sentence of Section 2.1 ("The severity classifications in this Section 2.1 apply for all purposes of the Agreement").
- This conflicts with D1 Section 1.11.
- D1 Section 17.4 resolves the conflict in the SLA Schedule's favor.

**What the drafts say:**

| Source | "Severity 1 Incident" |
|---|---|
| D1 § 1.11 (and term sheet § 5.2) | An incident making matchmaking, login **or** in-game purchases unavailable to **10% or more of End Users** |
| D4 § 2.1(a) | An incident resulting in the **complete unavailability of the Platform to all End Users in all regions** |

D4 Section 2.1(b) then pushes everything else into Severity 2. This expressly includes "an outage confined to one or more Regions, or to one or more first-party platforms." D1 Section 17.4 gives the SLA Schedule priority "as to … incident classification," so the D4 definition controls.

**Why it matters for Fatesk:**

- **Realistic outages never qualify.** A login-only outage, a storefront failure during a launch, or a full North America East outage would not be Severity 1, even if it hit far more than 10% of players. Only a simultaneous total outage across all five Regions qualifies. That scenario is rare.
- **The one-hour response obligation disappears in practice.** This covers D1 Section 7.2: one-hour response, continuous senior engineering and hourly updates. Severity 2 in D4 Section 4.1 allows a 2-hour response, 2-hourly updates and a 2-day resolution target.
- **Root cause analysis becomes optional.** The mandatory five-business-day RCA in D1 Section 7.4 becomes discretionary. D4 Section 4.4 provides a Severity 2 RCA only on request, in 10 business days.
- **The termination right is effectively lost.** The chronic-failure termination right in D1 Section 8.4 requires three Severity 1 Incidents in a rolling 90 days. That right with refund of prepaid fees is Fatesk's main exit from a failing platform, and under the D4 definition it is close to illusory.
- **The force majeure carve-out shrinks.** Under D1 Section 17.5, force majeure does not excuse Section 7.2. That protection now covers only total outages.
- **Escalation and the SOW acceptance test are affected.** D4 Section 3.3 escalates Severity 1 to Level 2 immediately, and that now applies only to total outages. The SOW Section 4.1(a) acceptance test ("no open Severity 1 or Severity 2 defects") is affected less, because Severity 2 is still captured.

This is a direct departure from term sheet Sections 5.2 to 5.4, which used the 10% definition.

**Recommended fix (in order of preference):**

1. Conform D4 Section 2.1(a) to D1:
   > "**Severity 1 Incident**" has the meaning given in Section 1.11 of the Agreement, and includes any incident making matchmaking, player login and authentication, or in-game commerce and storefront services (including entitlement grants and virtual currency balances) unavailable to 10% or more of End Users, whether across all Regions or within any one or more Regions or first-party platforms.

   Conform Section 2.1(b) so that Severity 2 begins below that threshold.
2. Delete the final sentence of D4 Section 2.1, or replace it with: "In the event of any inconsistency, the definition of Severity 1 Incident in Section 1.11 of the Agreement shall prevail."
3. Amend D1 Section 17.4 to add: "provided that the definition of Severity 1 Incident in Section 1.11, and Sections 7.2, 7.4 and 8.4, shall prevail over any conflicting provision of the SLA Schedule."

Also consider measuring the "10% of End Users" threshold per Licensed Title. A total outage of *Project Halcyon* at launch may be less than 10% of all End Users across the portfolio (see open question 5.2).

---

### Issue 2: California law and San Francisco forum in the SOW override the Delaware choice

**Where it appears:**
- D2 (SOW) Section 9.1 (governing law: "the laws of the State of California") and Section 9.2 (exclusive jurisdiction of "the state and federal courts located in San Francisco County, California").
- This conflicts with D1 Sections 17.1 (Delaware law) and 17.2 (exclusive jurisdiction of state and federal courts in Wilmington, Delaware).

**Why the conflict is not cured:** D1 Section 17.4 makes the SOW prevail "as to Implementation Services." SOW Section 9 expressly reaches "any dispute arising out of or relating to this SOW or the Implementation Services." Read together, the California choice controls implementation disputes. Delaware law and forum control everything else.

The term sheet (Section 12) agreed Delaware law and Wilmington courts for all of the Definitive Agreements. Neither party is a California entity: both are Delaware entities, and Drupuv is based in Austin. Nothing in the deal explains the California choice.

**Why it matters for Fatesk:**

- **The likely disputes straddle both documents.** Implementation Services include the following, all tied tightly to how the Platform performs:
  - SDK integration (D2 § 2.2);
  - migration of *Ironveil: Frontier* accounts, entitlements and virtual currency balances (D2 § 2.3); and
  - launch readiness and load testing at the Licensed Concurrency (D2 § 2.4).

  Take a failed launch, for example. It may involve:
  - an integration defect (SOW, so California);
  - a Platform warranty breach (D1 § 13.2(a), so Delaware);
  - a services warranty breach (D1 § 13.2(b), incorporated by SOW § 10.3, so the forum is arguable);
  - SLA failures and service credits (D1/D4, so Delaware); and
  - a data-migration loss of Fatesk Data (D1 § 9 via SOW § 8.4, so the forum is arguable).
- **Each forum is exclusive.** Fatesk could face two lawsuits on one set of facts, inconsistent rulings and threshold motion practice over which clause governs each claim. That adds cost and delay at the moment Fatesk most needs leverage.
- **It may help Drupuv to argue over forum.** Drupuv could use the forum fight to slow or fragment a claim, and to argue that California law applies to issues such as the services warranty or limitation of liability as applied to implementation claims.
- **Fatesk loses its home forum.** Wilmington is where Fatesk is headquartered, and the client wanted that forum.

**Recommended fix:**

1. **Preferred:** Replace SOW Section 9 with:
   > "This SOW is governed by, and any dispute arising out of or relating to this SOW or the Implementation Services shall be resolved in accordance with, Sections 17.1 and 17.2 of the Agreement."
2. **Belt and braces:** Amend D1 Section 17.4 to provide that "the SOW shall not prevail over Sections 14, 17.1 or 17.2 of this Agreement, and no SOW may vary the governing law, forum or limitation of liability provisions of this Agreement unless it expressly refers to and amends this Section 17.4." This also protects against future SOWs, which D1 Section 1.13 contemplates.
3. Raise the point with Drupuv as a term sheet conformity point rather than a new ask. It should be low-cost for Drupuv to concede.

---

### Issue 3: Three-year automatic renewal with a narrow 30-day notice window

**Where it appears:** D1 Section 12.2, read with Sections 12.1 and 5.3. It departs from term sheet Section 8.2.

**What the drafts say:**
- **Initial Term:** three years from February 1, 2027, which ends January 31, 2030 (D1 § 12.1).
- **Renewal:** the Agreement "shall renew automatically for successive three (3) year Renewal Terms."
- **Notice window:** a non-renewal notice is effective only if delivered "no earlier than one hundred fifty (150) days and no later than one hundred twenty (120) days before the end of the then-current term." That is a 30-day window. For the Initial Term it runs roughly September 3 to October 3, 2029 (exact dates to be confirmed).
- **Term sheet:** "one-year renewals; either party may decline renewal on 90 days' notice before term end."

**Why it matters for Fatesk:**

- **Missing the window is costly.** If Fatesk misses the 30-day window, early or late, it is locked in for three more years. At the $1,840,000 annual license fee that is about $5.52 million. If Drupuv applies the full 9% renewal increase permitted by D1 Section 5.3, it is about $6.02 million ($2,005,600 per year).
- **There is no termination for convenience.** The only exits are for cause (D1 § 12.3), insolvency (§ 12.4) and chronic failure (§ 8.4). Under Issue 1, the chronic-failure exit is currently largely illusory.
- **The early cut-off is a trap.** An early notice is ineffective, which is unusual. A notice sent in good faith 6 months out would not work.
- **Live-service planning needs flexibility.** Titles can be sunset or migrated, and a three-year lock-in limits Fatesk's ability to move to a competing backend or bring services in-house.
- **The fee-increase notice comes too late to rely on.** D1 Section 5.3 requires Drupuv to give notice of a renewal fee increase 180 days before the Renewal Term. That is *before* the non-renewal window opens, which is helpful. But Fatesk has no right to decline renewal specifically because of the increase, other than through the same narrow window.

**Recommended fix:**

1. Revise D1 Section 12.2 to the term sheet position:
